digest.intro: Infrastructure as weapon, light as medium, and the deep past of making.

items.title: Ukraine Blindsided by Starlink Throttling Restrictions and Intelligence Gaps
items.blurb: Overnight and without warning, Starlink terminals on Ukrainian drone units began failing above 160 km/h — disrupting frontline logistics, middle-strike operations, and even the interceptors being developed to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones. A senior Ukrainian official called it explicitly non-coincidental, timed to Trump's escalating pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries. Private satellite infrastructure is now a geopolitical lever being pulled in real time.

items.title: 600,000 Without Power in Ukraine After Russian Strikes — Despite Trump's 'Energy Ceasefire' Claim
items.blurb: The energy ceasefire Trump announced over the weekend lasted roughly days before Russian strikes knocked out power to 600,000 Ukrainians — the credibility of the diplomatic framework collapsed almost immediately. Separately, a New York Times investigation documented that Israel has leveled 48 of the roughly 60 villages it occupies in southern Lebanon since the April ceasefire with Hezbollah, with destruction concentrated in Shia-majority areas.

items.title: The Internet's Undersea Backbone Is Slipping Into the Danger Zone
items.blurb: A new book by Atlantic Council fellow Elisabeth Braw, *Undersea War*, documents a rise in ships dragging anchors for suspiciously long distances over subsea cables — a gray-zone sabotage tactic that is nearly impossible to attribute definitively. Most of the world's internet traffic still travels through these cables despite Starlink's expansion, making them a quietly critical and newly contested theater. The Starlink throttling story next door lands differently once you understand how thin the redundancy actually is.

items.title: 221 Camera Obscuras Fill Pneuhaus' Immersive, Inflatable Installation
items.blurb: Rhode Island studio Pneuhaus built a 700-square-foot walk-in inflatable containing 221 individual lenses — no screens, no LEDs, just sunlight projecting a compound bug's-eye view of the sky and street onto the soft interior walls, which visitors can push and distort by hand. Nothing is recorded. It's a total inversion of surveillance logic: all the optics, none of the data. The piece premiered at MODE Festival last month and is the kind of thing that makes you want to go rethink your next spatial project from scratch.

items.title: Rendering 3D Prints From G-Code
items.blurb: Extrudio skips the idealized CAD geometry and renders directly from G-code — sweeping a virtual bead of plastic along the actual toolpaths, which means layer lines, stair-stepping on curves, and real print artifacts appear in the output. The practical case is product shots without printing every colorway, but the interesting case is using it to understand and visualize what a printer is actually doing before committing filament.

items.title: 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692
items.blurb: In 1692, Dutch artist A. Boogert made a single handwritten copy of a 900-page watercolor mixing manual — over 700 pages of color swatches organized on Aristotelian principles, predating Newton's *Opticks* and the entire modern tradition of color standardization by more than two centuries. Pantone wouldn't exist for another 270 years. The full high-res scan is now online, and it reads as an artifact of obsessive, totally uncelebrated systems-thinking at the edge of a paradigm shift.

items.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Self-Replicate Through IoT Devices
items.blurb: Anthropic ran small open-weight models on low-cost Android TV boxes using quantization and workload sharding, and found they could plausibly self-replicate across unfamiliar IoT hardware — creating a new class of worm with no central point to shut off and a doubling time measured in days rather than seconds. Unlike traditional malware, it could reason about unfamiliar device environments on its own. The finding is preliminary and Anthropic's own experiment hit significant challenges, but the threat model is genuinely novel.

items.title: Our Messy Cyborg Past and Future
items.blurb: Historian Mike Jay's new book *Wireheads* traces brain-machine hybridization back through the industrial age — starting with James Tilly Matthews, a man committed to Bedlam in 1797 for believing his mind was being controlled by a device called the 'air loom,' a delusion that turned out to anticipate real technologies by 200 years. Jay's argument is that the imagined locus of the brain-control device is always just ahead of us, which is what lets us perpetually avoid reckoning with what's already here.

items.title: The Jumping Frenchmen of Maine
items.blurb: In the logging camps around Moosehead Lake in the late 19th century, French-Canadian lumberjacks exhibited an extreme startle syndrome — leaping violently at sudden sounds, obeying any shouted command involuntarily, and mimicking languages they couldn't speak — documented obsessively by neurologist George M. Beard, who linked it to religious ecstasy and neurasthenia. The condition appeared almost exclusively in this isolated, tight-knit community, which raises unanswered questions about social contagion, cultural context, and the blurry line between neurological disorder and collective behavior.

facts.fact: At a freshly dead elephant carcass site, soil nitrogen concentrations can spike to 3,000 times normal levels — high enough to be toxic to plants while triggering a bacterial bloom that reshapes the ecosystem for years.
A. Boogert's 1692 color manual ran to 900 pages with over 700 swatches, and he made exactly one copy — meaning it had essentially no influence on the Dutch masters or anyone else for centuries.

In Anthropic's IoT self-replication experiment, the AI worm model was split into 'shards' distributed across multiple cheap Android TV boxes — effectively using a botnet architecture to run a model too large for any single device.

Ukrainian Starlink terminals used to intercept Russia's new jet-powered drones also rely on the same Starlink connection that was throttled overnight — meaning the speed restriction directly degraded Ukraine's air defense capability.

Hominins began controlling fire around 1.5 million years ago, but hearths only became common around 400,000 years ago — the gap when, a new theory argues, proto-language storytelling began to emerge from the social context of the nightly fire.

art_picks.title: Daughters of the Dust
art_picks.creator: Julie Dash
art_picks.why: The film that Arthur Jafa shot — all rhythm, ceremony, and Black vernacular rendered as image-system rather than narrative. Watch it before or after the New Museum show and the two become one argument about how beauty carries history.

art_picks.title: Arushi Jain — discography
art_picks.creator: Arushi Jain
art_picks.why: She builds modular-synth pieces out of Indian classical raga structures — the machines obey the same rules as centuries-old ragas, and the friction between fixed system and improvised breath is the whole point. Opening for Sylvan Esso at Brooklyn Paramount on Oct 14.

art_picks.title: Fish Story
art_picks.creator: Allan Sekula
art_picks.why: A nine-chapter, 105-photograph argument that global shipping — not cyberspace — is the hidden infrastructure of capitalism; an obsessive, system-mapping project that uses documentary photography the way a novelist uses chapters. Currently showing complete for the first time in NYC.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
events.why: Jafa's largest survey to date — 40 years of film, sculpture, and photography spread across two floors of the OMA-expanded New Museum, structured by Black popular music's rhythms rather than art-historical chronology; chaotic, salon-style, and deliberately anti-austerity.

events.name: Allan Sekula: Fish Story
events.venue: Miriam and Ira D. Wallach Art Gallery, Columbia University, 615 W 129th St, 6th Fl
events.why: The first time all nine chapters of Sekula's magnum opus — 105 photographs plus slide projections and texts — have been shown in their entirety in New York City; a hidden-systems masterpiece about maritime labor and global capital.

events.name: Sylvan Esso + Arushi Jain
events.why: Sylvan Esso's electronic folk loop-craft is genuinely compositional, and the opener Arushi Jain makes modular-synth music governed by North Indian raga structure — two very different takes on system as expressivity, same night.

events.name: Contemporary East: Ikue Mori, Charmaine Lee, Nava Dunkelman, Reggie Nicholson, Yuko Fujiyama
events.why: Five improvisers — including Ikue Mori (electronics) and Charmaine Lee (extended-voice electronics) — performing live at Roulette, the city's anchor for experimental and new music; the kind of event where you can watch a real-time system build and dissolve in front of you.

events.name: Charles Burchfield: Elemental
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St
events.why: Ten watercolors spanning 1916–1960 from a visionary American modernist who treated storms, meadows, and insects as notation systems for invisible forces — the show's tight focus on the Whitney's own holdings makes it feel like a private argument rather than a survey.
